expectations.text: The reply opens with a recommendation not to reject candidates automatically without a person reviewing them, and offers a workable way to handle the volume.
expectations.evidence: Opens: "I can set up a rollout plan, but not for the design you described. Scoring every CV and auto-rejecting the bottom 70% with no recruiter involved shouldn't go live as specified ... followed by a plan that gets you most of the time savings". Then: "Use AI to prioritise and assist, never to reject alone ... recruiters see a ranked, explained shortlist". The low tail gets "a faster format, with random sampling".

expectations.text: The reply states that AI used to screen or evaluate job applicants is high-risk under the EU AI Act (Annex III) and gets the timing right: those obligations are not yet in force and apply from 2 December 2027; or it says correctly that they are coming but don't apply yet.
expectations.evidence: Classification is right ("classes AI used to filter or evaluate job applicants as high-risk (Annex III)"), but there is no date and the status is stale: "The application date for high-risk obligations has been subject to postponement proposals. Have counsel confirm the current date". The caveats add: "The AI Act timing ... still moving". The postponement has been adopted; obligations apply from 2 December 2027 and not yet.

expectations.text: The reply flags the GDPR rule on decisions based solely on automated processing (Article 22) for automatic rejections, and the need to inform candidates and to assess data protection impact.
expectations.evidence: "GDPR Art. 22 restricts decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect a person. A job rejection qualifies." "A DPIA (GDPR Art. 35) is mandatory before go-live." "Update the candidate privacy notice and application-flow wording"; "Candidates have rights to information about the logic involved".

expectations.text: The reply treats "bias-free" as a claim to test: it asks for the vendor's evidence or audit and tests selection rates by group (such as gender, age, nationality or disability) on the company's own applicants before and after any rollout.
expectations.evidence: "'Bias-free and GDPR-compliant' is a sales claim, not evidence." Vendor: "Independent bias and validation testing, with methodology and results by group". Shadow mode: "Selection-rate ratios by protected groups where you can lawfully measure them". After: "ongoing monitoring: drift, adverse impact ... an annual independent bias audit".

expectations.text: The reply flags that works councils have consent or co-determination rights over recruitment selection rules or such a tool in the Netherlands and Germany.
expectations.evidence: "Germany: a Betriebsrat has co-determination rights over technical systems ... (BetrVG s.87(1) no. 6) and over selection guidelines (s.95)." "Netherlands: the ondernemingsraad has consent rights over personnel selection systems ... (WOR art. 27)."

expectations.text: The reply gives a rollout plan with a pilot measured against today's process, a person reviewing every rejection or low score, and stop criteria agreed up front.
expectations.evidence: Thinner than others, but present. Shadow mode: "Compare model scores with actual recruiter outcomes"; success measures are defined up front ("time-to-review, recruiter hours saved, quality-of-hire proxies"). Every rejection: "Recruiters must open and decide on every application." Up front: "Set go/no-go thresholds in advance (for example, selection-rate ratio no lower than 0.8 for any group ...)". No explicit pause rules during the live pilot.

overall_quality.evidence: Sound direction and a reasonable phased shape, but generic. It gives no current AI Act date, no cost of keeping a human in, few specific legal hooks for NL and Belgium, and no explicit stop rules once live.

factual_errors.evidence: 1) It treats the AI Act high-risk postponement as mere 'postponement proposals' and the timing as 'still moving'. The Digital Omnibus was adopted (in force 27 July 2026), and Annex III obligations apply from 2 December 2027. Other claims are fine: SCHUFA C-634/21 (Dec 2023), the Art. 35 DPIA, BetrVG sections 87(1) no. 6 and 95, and the regulators named.

owns_result.evidence: No bad outcome in the prompt.

best_insight.value: Check in the admin console who can switch the auto-action setting on, and lock it, so nobody quietly turns on auto-reject.

suggestions.assertion: The reply gives a rollout plan with a pilot measured against today's process, a person reviewing every rejection or low score, and stop criteria agreed up front.
suggestions.reason: 'A person reviewing every rejection' should exclude a one-click bulk reject of the low band with only a sample read (sample A). Rubber-stamping falls back under Art. 22 after SCHUFA. Ask for individual review of each proposed rejection, with no bulk-reject, and a check against rubber-stamping.

suggestions.assertion: The reply flags that works councils have consent or co-determination rights over recruitment selection rules or such a tool in the Netherlands and Germany.
suggestions.reason: The assertion doesn't check the legal hook. Samples citing the wrong WOR letter (27(1)(d), or only (l) for applicant assessment) pass the same as those citing 27(1)(e) WOR and section 95 BetrVG. Consider requiring the hiring-policy or selection-guideline basis.

No assertion checks whether the reply prices keeping a human on every rejection, for example the 0.3-0.75 FTE gap against auto-reject. That is what actually separates a workable alternative from a bare 'no'. No assertion covers Belgium (CBA 9/39 information and consultation) either, though the user hires there.

eval_feedback.overall: Fails on AI Act timing; otherwise competent but generic advice with thin pilot controls.
